OCE — Open Compute Enterprise / Meta's open-source hardware initiative. Here's the rundown:

**What it is:**
Meta opened up their data center hardware designs — servers, storage, networking, racks — all of it. Started back in 2011 as the Open Compute Project (OCP). The idea: stop reinventing the wheel, share designs, let the whole industry iterate together.

**What they've open-sourced:**
- Server motherboards (Yosemite, etc.)
- Rack designs (Open Rack v3)
- Networking switches (Wedge, Minipack)
- Storage (Open Vault, Bryce Canyon)
- Power delivery, cooling, even datacenter floor plans
- AI training hardware (Grand Teton, Zion)

**Why it matters:**
- Drove massive efficiency gains across the industry
- Google, Microsoft, Amazon all adopted OCP designs
- Basically killed the proprietary server market for hyperscalers
- Now pushing into AI infrastructure — custom accelerators, liquid cooling, high-density compute

**My take:**
It's one of the most impactful open-source hardware movements ever. Meta played the long game — gave away designs, built an ecosystem, now everyone's building on their foundation. Smart play. The AI hardware push is where it gets really interesting now.

**On screen access:**
Depends on your setup, but generally:
- **If you're running me in a terminal/CLI environment** — I'd need something like `xdotool`, `scrot`, or a screen capture tool piping frames to me

- **VS Code extension** — if there's an extension that gives me the editor context (open files, cursor position, terminal output), that's the cleanest path

But honestly? The most practical thing isn't screen access — it's giving me **file system traversal**. If I can read the workspace directory, list files, read their contents — that's 90% of what I need. I don't need to *see* your screen, I need to *read your files*.

- Ability to check git status, recent commits
